english: If you are unsure, learn the Israeli-based sounds first. They are what the Hebrew of Israel uses and what most non-Orthodox respondents in the survey reported, and the Ashkenazi switches (tav, kamatz, cholam, tsere, stress) can be added afterwards.

english:
A Reform synagogue in the US (suggested setting: sephardi; confidence medium)
Most likely Israeli-based sounds, which the app calls the American-synagogue setting. Expect some Ashkenazi forms in familiar words and songs.
Caveats: In the survey, Reform respondents were the group most likely to choose the Israeli form of the one word asked about, but about a third also use the Ashkenazic form. Individual cantors and older members often keep Ashkenazi habits.
Ask first: Which pronunciation do the cantor and the Torah readers use, and is there a recording I can practise with?
what_to_check: Does this description of what congregations of this kind usually do match your experience? Anything unfair to a stream or community? (Evidence behind it is thin; the guide says so.)

english:
A Conservative synagogue in the US (suggested setting: sephardi; confidence medium)
Again, Israeli-based sounds are the more common choice in the survey, with a large Ashkenazic minority. Congregations differ.
Caveats: One word measured: 73% chose the Israeli form, 34% the Ashkenazic form. Congregations differ, and the survey cannot tell you which kind yours is.
Ask first: Does the shul use Israeli-style pronunciation for Torah reading and for the siddur, or does it differ between the two?
what_to_check: Does this description of what congregations of this kind usually do match your experience? Anything unfair to a stream or community? (Evidence behind it is thin; the guide says so.)

english:
A Modern Orthodox synagogue in the US (suggested setting: sephardi; confidence low)
Mixed. The survey found both forms common (70% Israeli, 47% Ashkenazic for the one word). Listen first.
Caveats: Many Modern Orthodox people switch between forms depending on setting. Torah reading and prayer may use a different pronunciation from everyday Hebrew words.
Ask first: What do the rabbi and the baal koreh (Torah reader) use?
what_to_check: Does this description of what congregations of this kind usually do match your experience? Anything unfair to a stream or community? (Evidence behind it is thin; the guide says so.)

english:
An Orthodox or Haredi synagogue in the US (suggested setting: ashkenazi; confidence low)
Ashkenazi pronunciation is more common here than elsewhere in the survey, but not universal. Half of the Orthodox respondents also reported the Israeli form, so Israeli-style and Sephardi communities exist inside Orthodoxy too.
Caveats: Survey: 67% (Orthodox) and 73% (Black Hat) chose the Ashkenazic form of the one word, yet 50% and 38% chose the Israeli form. Ashkenazi has regional dialects. ALEF models one common siddur style; your community's may differ (for example oy or ey for cholam).
Ask first: Which dialect of Ashkenazi does my community use, and who can I copy?
what_to_check: Does this description of what congregations of this kind usually do match your experience? Anything unfair to a stream or community? (Evidence behind it is thin; the guide says so.)

english:
A Sephardi, Mizrahi or other non-Ashkenazi community (suggested setting: sephardi; confidence medium)
The app's Sephardi-values setting matches the vowels (a, e, i, o, u) but not your community's consonants, which may include pharyngeal het and ayin.
Caveats: 'Sephardi' covers many communities with different habits (Spanish-Portuguese, North African, Balkan, Levantine, Iraqi, Yemenite and more). ALEF does not model any of them in detail. Use it for reading practice and take the sounds from a member of your community.
Ask first: Can someone from my community record or sit with me for the throat sounds and for how they say the prayers?
what_to_check: Does this description of what congregations of this kind usually do match your experience? Anything unfair to a stream or community? (Evidence behind it is thin; the guide says so.)

english:
Preparing to read Torah or lead prayers (for example for a bar or bat mitzvah) (suggested setting: null; confidence medium)
Use the tradition your synagogue and teacher use. That choice is made by your community, not by this app.
Caveats: Cantillation (the trope melodies) is a separate topic not taught here. Take the recording or the teacher's reading as the final authority for your congregation.
Ask first: Which pronunciation and which melodies does my teacher expect?

english:
Travelling or living in Israel (suggested setting: israeli; confidence high)
Learn the Modern Israeli sounds. Everyday Israeli Hebrew has no pharyngeals for most speakers, a back-of-the-throat r, and mostly final stress.
Caveats: Some older Mizrahi Israelis still use pharyngeal sounds, and Israeli synagogues keep Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi and Yemenite customs side by side. ALEF does not teach Tel Aviv slang or informal fast speech: no source for those was found.
Ask first: Is it for travel talk (Israeli track) or for services in Israel (ask the synagogue)?

english:
Tav without a dot (ת) (Shabbat / Shabbos)
Israeli: t (Shabbat)
American synagogue: t in most non-Orthodox practice (Shabbat). Orthodox and Ashkenazi-leaning synagogues often say s (Shabbos).
Ashkenazi: s (Shabbos, Yis-gadal)
Other communities: Yemenite, Iraqi and some Greek communities: th as in thin; some Spanish-Portuguese and Spanish-Moroccan communities: d, or th as in this
what_to_check: Per-sound comparison across settings (confidence claimed: high). Read the example word aloud in each setting: are the cells right? Are the "other communities" claims right?

english:
Kamatz (T-shaped mark) (barukh / borukh)
Israeli: ah, as in father
American synagogue: ah, as in father. Some older or Orthodox speakers say aw.
Ashkenazi: o or aw (Borukh). Southern Ashkenazi dialects use u when the syllable is open.
Other communities: Sephardi (popular speech): ah, the same as patach; Yemenite: a back, rounded vowel like the Ashkenazi o (per the Ashkenazi Hebrew page)
what_to_check: Per-sound comparison across settings (confidence claimed: high). Read the example word aloud in each setting: are the cells right? Are the "other communities" claims right?

english:
Patach and kamatz: same vowel or two? (atah / atoh)
Israeli: Same: both are ah.
American synagogue: Same: both are ah.
Ashkenazi: Two vowels: patach is ah, kamatz is o or aw.
Other communities: Sephardi (popular speech): Same: both ah. The page adds that formal liturgical reading often restores a distinction (it does not say how).; Yemenite: Kept apart; patach and segol sound alike
what_to_check: Per-sound comparison across settings (confidence claimed: high). Read the example word aloud in each setting: are the cells right? Are the "other communities" claims right?

english:
Cholam (dot above) (shalom / sholom)
Israeli: oh
American synagogue: oh
Ashkenazi: varies by region: oh (southern German), oy (Polish/Galician), ey (Lithuanian), ow (northern German). The app's siddur style writes plain o.
Other communities: Sephardi: oh
what_to_check: Per-sound comparison across settings (confidence claimed: high). Read the example word aloud in each setting: are the cells right? Are the "other communities" claims right?

english:
Tsere (two dots) and segol (three dots) (amen / omeyn)
Israeli: eh, as in bed. Some speakers say ey in some words.
American synagogue: eh, often stretched into an ay glide (HAY-nu).
Ashkenazi: ey, as in they (some Polish usage: ai)
Other communities: Sephardi: eh; tsere and segol sound the same
what_to_check: Per-sound comparison across settings (confidence claimed: high). Read the example word aloud in each setting: are the cells right? Are the "other communities" claims right?

english:
Shva (two dots, stacked) (brakha / bruhkhah)
Israeli: a quick e, or nothing at all in everyday speech
American synagogue: a quick e when reading prayers
Ashkenazi: often dropped in speech; read as a short e or uh when reading liturgy strictly
Other communities: Sephardi: a short e in every position where it is sounded; always sounded after a long vowel
what_to_check: Per-sound comparison across settings (confidence claimed: medium). Read the example word aloud in each setting: are the cells right? Are the "other communities" claims right?

english:
Ayin (ע) (olam / oylom)
Israeli: silent, or a tiny catch like the break in uh-oh (same as alef)
American synagogue: silent
Ashkenazi: silent in most forms. Traditional authorities advised a throaty sound in prayer, which is rarely done.
Other communities: Balkan, Anatolian, North African and Levantine Sephardim: a throaty, Arabic-like pharyngeal sound; Yemenite: the same pharyngeal sound; Older Mizrahi speakers in Israel: sometimes keep it, less often than het; Western Sephardim (Spanish-Portuguese): an ng sound as in singing
what_to_check: Per-sound comparison across settings (confidence claimed: high). Read the example word aloud in each setting: are the cells right? Are the "other communities" claims right?

english:
Chet (ח) versus khaf (כ without dot) (challah)
Israeli: ch as in Scottish loch, the same sound as khaf
American synagogue: ch as in Bach for both (the usual habit); some say a plain h, which is a slip to fix
Ashkenazi: ch as in Bach, the same as khaf. A throaty sound was advised but is rarely heard.
Other communities: Sephardim and Mizrahim who keep it, and Yemenite: a pharyngeal, throaty h that differs from khaf; Older Mizrahi speakers in Israel: often keep the pharyngeal
what_to_check: Per-sound comparison across settings (confidence claimed: high). Read the example word aloud in each setting: are the cells right? Are the "other communities" claims right?

english:
Qof (ק) (kadosh / kodoysh)
Israeli: k, the same as kaf with a dot
American synagogue: k
Ashkenazi: k
Other communities: Sephardi (general table): k; Georgian Jewish liturgical tradition: kept distinct from kaf with a dot, as in Arabic
what_to_check: Per-sound comparison across settings (confidence claimed: medium). Read the example word aloud in each setting: are the cells right? Are the "other communities" claims right?

english:
Resh (ר) (Reuven)
Israeli: a back-of-the-throat r, like French or German; nearly all Israeli Jews use it
American synagogue: the English r (most Americans). Hearing a uvular r in Israel is normal; using the English r is a common marker of a foreign speaker (lane 3's inference).
Ashkenazi: a tapped or trilled r or a uvular r, depending on region
Other communities: Sephardi: a front tapped or trilled r, like Spanish; Immigrants from Arabic-speaking countries (Israel): often keep the trilled r
what_to_check: Per-sound comparison across settings (confidence claimed: high). Read the example word aloud in each setting: are the cells right? Are the "other communities" claims right?

english:
Which syllable is stressed (shaLOM / SHOlom)
Israeli: most words on the last syllable; some, such as words of the melech/boker type, on the one before; spoken Israeli drifts toward the second-to-last syllable
American synagogue: last syllable in prayer words (baRUKH, shaLOM), as in Israeli
Ashkenazi: traditionally the second-to-last syllable (SHOlom, BOrukh), but final stress was promoted for Torah reading and public prayer, and many congregations use it
Other communities: Sephardi: keeps the older pattern, which for most words is the last syllable; Yemenite: the Wikipedia page says second-to-last, but tags that claim 'citation needed'; ALEF does not rely on it
what_to_check: Per-sound comparison across settings (confidence claimed: medium). Read the example word aloud in each setting: are the cells right? Are the "other communities" claims right?

english:
Yemenite Hebrew
Pharyngeal het and ayin, as in Arabic.
Gimel without a dot is a voiced throat fricative and with a dot is a j sound.
Tav without a dot is th as in thin; dalet without a dot is th as in this.
Patach and segol sound alike.
Described by one Wikipedia article only (first 100,000 of 124,343 characters read). ALEF has no Yemenite audio, respelling or lesson; this is a note that it exists.
what_to_check: Claims about another community's pronunciation (from one Wikipedia article). Are they accurate and respectfully put?

english:
Mizrahi and Sephardi communities (Middle East, North Africa, Balkans, Anatolia)
Many keep pharyngeal het and sometimes ayin; the details differ by community.
Some read tav as th, and some keep qof distinct (the pages we read name Iraqi, Greek and Georgian examples).
There is no single 'Sephardi accent': the pages stress many variants inside each grouping.
ALEF's 'sephardi' setting is NOT a model of any of these communities. If your synagogue belongs to one, ask a member or the cantor and treat this app as a general guide only.
